name: Elena Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior designer at Paper Kite, a little agency of six that makes social media ads and shop branding for local businesses: cafés, a climbing gym, two hairdressers, a vet. My day starts with a stand-up call at half nine, then I build ad sets, usually ten or fifteen versions of the same idea for different screens. I use AI tools all day, for first drafts of images, for writing alt text, for cutting out photos. My boss, Hana, says I'm the fastest at producing and the weakest at judging what's good, which is fair.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love trying new tools. When a new image model comes out I'm testing it that night with a cup of noodles. What wears me out is that the ads only live for a week, so nothing I make lasts. And clients ask for something 'like what the big brands do' on a tiny budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that the tools are useful but they aren't magic. I'd post a thread about which ones are actually worth paying for. At work I'd tease the people who were scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed, because I like the tools. But for my job, it's fine. I'd keep my edge as the person who's quick with them, and I'd have time to get better at the judging part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and ask Hana to let me sit on a real branding project, start to finish. I'd take an online course in art direction, maybe the one that costs six hundred. And I'd keep putting a bit into my index fund each month, like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, but calm. My job and my savings are fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing you make lasts. Does that matter in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters to me more than the tech does. I'd like to make a logo that's on a shop sign for twenty years. In a slow world, I've got the time to learn how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything worrying you outside work in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, a bit. Joy, my flatmate, wants to move in with her boyfriend next year, so I'd need a new flatmate or a smaller place. But I've got about ten months saved, so it's an annoyance, not a crisis.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful but not magic**.
I'd post a thread on which tools are **worth paying for**.
think: I'm **a bit disappointed**, because I enjoy the tools.
My **edge with the tools** stays, and I'd get time to improve my judgement.
do: Ask my boss for a full **branding project**, start to finish.
Take a **six-hundred** online course in art direction.
Keep adding monthly to my **index fund**.
feel: **Calm**, slightly **let down** that the tools stall.
S0.quote: I'd like to make a logo that's on a shop sign for twenty years.
fieldNote: She's **disappointed** by a plateau, unlike most, because she enjoys the tools.
Her real hunger is for **lasting work**, not faster output.
A flatmate leaving is a **minor pressure** her **savings** easily absorb.

steps.text: Ask Hana to put her on a full branding project
Take a six-hundred online course in art direction
Keep adding to the index fund every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that this is the moment to share the gains. If AI makes a six-person studio do the work of twelve, the six should get shorter weeks, not a layoff. I'd say that at work and online, a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm safer than most juniors, because I'm already the AI person at Paper Kite. But I also know I'm weak at taste, and the tools are getting better at taste too. So I'm safe for now, not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person who sets up Paper Kite's AI workflow, the templates and checks, so the whole team is faster. I'd ask for that to be in my job title, with a raise. I'd join the creative workers' union, too, because I'd want to be on the side pushing for shorter weeks. And on the side I'd start teaching evening workshops on the tools for small business owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job looks safe, maybe safer. But friends from college are losing freelance work, and I think about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which friends are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam from my course does illustration for children's books, and those jobs are drying up already. Kofi does wedding stationery. I'd be the one with the job, and that's awkward at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't there a contradiction, making the team faster while worrying about jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, there is, and I've thought about it. If I don't build the workflow, Hana buys one from a software firm and nobody gets a say. I'd rather be inside the room, pushing for shorter weeks.

say: I'd say we must **share the gains**, with shorter weeks instead of layoffs.
I'd repeat it **at work and online**.
think: I'm **safer than most juniors**, being the agency's AI person.
The tools are improving at **taste**, my weak spot, so I'm **not safe forever**.
do: Build the agency's **AI workflow** and ask for a title change and a **raise**.
Join the **creative workers' union** to push for shorter weeks.
Teach **evening workshops** on AI tools for small business owners.
feel: **Uneasy**, safe herself but **thinking of friends** losing freelance work.
S1.quote: If AI makes a six-person studio do the work of twelve, the six should get shorter weeks, not a layoff.
fieldNote: She sees **building the workflow** herself as better than a bought one.
She names a **contradiction** openly and resolves it as being **inside the room**.
Her **guilt** about friends shapes her public push for shared gains.

steps.text: Build Paper Kite's AI templates and checks for the team
Ask Hana for an AI workflow title and a raise
Teach paid evening AI workshops for small business owners

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that we need a basic income, now, before the shock lands. I'd post about it every day. At work I'd say let's talk about what Paper Kite even is in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is the one that hits me hardest, because I see the tools every day. I know how fast they're getting better. My whole value is being quick with tools, and AGI by 2028 means anyone can be quick with them, including the clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd set up a small design co-op with Sam and Kofi, so at least we're owners and not just staff. I'd move part of my savings into a cheaper flat share to make the money last longer. In the three years before robots, I'd look at hands-on work linked to design, like painting shop signs or building window displays. And I'd volunteer for a basic income campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake. I'm usually the excited one, and I wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work is almost all screen, so the gap barely helps me directly. It helps if I jump into window displays and shop signs, because those need hands, ladders and paint. But I'd be learning a trade at 28 to keep it maybe three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring my mum and tell her not to worry, I've got ten months saved. Then I'd hang up and worry. She'd tell me to come home, and honestly, I might.

say: I'd demand a **basic income** now, before the shock lands.
At work I'd ask what the **agency even is** in two years.
think: I see the tools daily, so I know **how fast** they improve.
My value is **being quick** with tools, and AGI makes everyone quick.
do: Set up a **design co-op** with two college friends in the first months.
Move to a **cheaper flat share** to stretch savings.
Learn **window displays** and sign painting before robots arrive around 2031.
feel: **Alarmed** and lying awake, though she's usually **the excited one**.
S2.quote: My whole value is being quick with tools, and AGI by 2028 means anyone can be quick with them, including the clients.
fieldNote: Her daily use of AI makes her **more** alarmed here, not less.
The **robot lag** barely helps her screen-based job unless she switches.
She leans on **ownership** through a co-op and on a **basic income** campaign.
Moving home to her mum is a **quiet backup** she half admits.

steps.text: Start a small design co-op with Sam and Kofi
Move to a cheaper flat share to stretch savings
Learn window display building and sign painting
Volunteer for a basic income campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the fast one, I'd push for a basic income, but with five years I'd say there's time to design it well. I'd post less panic and more plans. At work I'd suggest we build a plan for Paper Kite as a team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to change what I am. I'd become someone who runs projects with AI rather than someone who makes the pixels. That still ends in 2031, but it buys good years and good savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Hana to train me in client management and art direction over the next two years. I'd keep the co-op idea going in the background with Sam and Kofi. I'd save harder, maybe a third of my pay, for the gap after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not alarmed, because I can see steps. But I'd still expect my design income to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: After AGI lands in 2031, what's left for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the bits with people in a room: running a workshop, sitting with a café owner deciding what their place feels like. That's thinking work too, though, so I'm honest that it's not safe. Then hands-on display work until robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tools are just tools. I'd blame a system where the gains go to a few companies, not the tools. I'd vote and campaign for that to change.

say: I'd push for a **basic income** designed well with time to plan.
I'd suggest a **team plan** for the agency.
think: Five years lets me **change what I am**.
I'd run projects with AI rather than make pixels, until **2031**.
do: Train in **client management** and art direction over two years.
Save about **a third of pay** for the gap after 2031.
Keep the **co-op** idea alive with friends.
S3.quote: I'd blame a system where the gains go to a few companies, not the tools.
fieldNote: Five years turns her alarm into **career redesign**.
She's honest that **people-facing** work is also thinking work.
She blames **who gets the gains**, not the technology itself.

steps.text: Train with Hana in client management and art direction
Save a third of each pay cheque
Keep planning the design co-op with Sam and Kofi
Campaign and vote for sharing AI gains more widely

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it properly: basic income trials, shorter weeks, training paid for by the companies making the money. I'd post about the trials in other places. At work I'd say let's enjoy the tools while making a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well for most of the decade. I'm good with the tools, and the gap between using them and not is where money is made. By 2036 I'd be 37 with a decade of savings and a co-op, and I think I could move into something with people or hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make Paper Kite's AI work my speciality for three or four years, and earn on it. I'd launch the co-op with Sam and Kofi by year three. I'd put more into my index fund, so there's a real cushion by 2036. And I'd look into a part-time course in exhibition design, which is half building things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's coming, but I feel like I'm ahead of it. My job looks safe for a good while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said the tools improve at taste. Doesn't that make ten years risky for you too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, in the end. But ten years is a long time to be useful. I'd rather have a decade of good work and a plan than spend ten years worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind and act faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Hana stopped hiring juniors at all. That would be my sign. Then I'd move the co-op forward by a couple of years.

say: I'd call ten years enough for **basic income trials** and shorter weeks.
At work I'd say **enjoy the tools** while making a plan.
think: I'd do **well for most** of the decade, being good with tools.
By **37** I'd have savings and a co-op to move with.
do: Make the agency's **AI work** my speciality for three or four years.
Launch the **co-op** by year three and grow the **index fund**.
S4.quote: I'd rather have a decade of good work and a plan than spend ten years worrying.
fieldNote: With a decade she feels **ahead**, and her mood drops to uneasy.
She names a clear **trigger**: her boss stopping junior hiring.
She mixes **investing**, a co-op and a hands-on course into one plan.

steps.text: Make AI production work her paid speciality at Paper Kite
Launch the design co-op with Sam and Kofi by year three
Put more into the index fund each month
Take a part-time exhibition design course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I use the tools every day, so I'd see it coming faster than anyone and still not have time. What would help is a basic income, even a small one, so people like me can retrain without burning through savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we'd lose. Being excited about AI and scared of it are both true for me. I'm the girl who tests every new image model at midnight, and I'm also the one who'd be replaced by it first.

headlineQuote: Being excited about AI and scared of it are both true for me.
portrait: Elena is a junior at a **six-person agency** making social ads for local firms.
She uses **AI tools daily** and is the agency's fastest producer but weakest judge.
She pushes for **shared gains**, shorter weeks and a **basic income**.
Her answers swing from **calm** in a plateau to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028.
Her plans centre on a **design co-op** with college friends and hands-on display work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd see it coming fastest yet still lack time.
whatWouldHelp: A small **basic income** so she could retrain without **burning savings**.
